h1:
Phichit Night Markets & Walking Streets
An Easy Evening of Grazing
intro: Phichit doesn't have big malls or a glossy dining district, but the charm of this town lives in its night markets and walking streets, which rotate open almost every day of the week. You can graze your way through hot rice-and-curry, freshly fried snacks, and the old-school local sweets of Chalawan town that get harder to find every year. We've rounded up the markets that actually open, which days and times, and the eats worth trying, all on one page.

blocks.html: If you arrive in Phichit in the evening, the best move is to find a market and just eat your way through it. The town has night markets and walking streets spread across the city center and the surrounding districts. Some open daily, others only on certain days of the week. The upside: the food is still down-to-earth, around 40–60 THB a plate is enough to fill you up, and you'll find local sweets that have all but disappeared in bigger cities. We've sorted them by opening day so it's easy to plan which night to go where.

blocks.text: Phichit night markets & walking streets worth visiting

blocks.html: Phichit's markets rotate through the week, and locals just know which day goes where. We've picked only the ones that still open for real and have enough food to make grazing worthwhile, ordered mainly by how convenient they are if you're staying in the city center.

items.name: Bang Khi Nak Walking Street (Bang Mun Nak)
items.blurb: One of Phichit's liveliest walking streets, set in a row of old wooden shophouses along the river in Bang Mun Nak district. It's a long walk with rice-and-curry, fried snacks, grilled street food, and local sweets, and the old-community atmosphere makes it more enjoyable to stroll than your average market. It's about 40 km from Phichit town, but worth it if your trip lands on a Saturday.
items.meta: Every Saturday · 2–8 pm · Bang Mun Nak district

items.name: Je Khiad Market, Sri Wanit (by the PTT station)
items.blurb: An evening market in town that draws plenty of locals. It's spacious with easy parking, mixing food, household goods, and clothes. You can graze from rice-and-curry to noodles and fried snacks, plus fruit and desserts. A solid, no-fuss dinner option if you're staying in town.

items.name: Wang Krot Old Market
items.blurb: A riverside old community on the Nan River dating to the reign of King Rama V that has become one of Phichit's go-to food spots. The draw is old-fashioned eats and local sweets among the wooden shophouses. Come midday to late afternoon for the full atmosphere, since many items sell out fast. Arrive before 3 pm if you want the full spread.
items.meta: Busiest Fri–Sat · late morning–afternoon · Mueang district

items.name: Phichit Thani Bus Terminal Market
items.blurb: A large market next to the bus terminal with loads of food, plenty of stalls, and cheap prices. Good for anyone who wants to browse a wide variety of eats in one place, from bagged home-style dishes to fried snacks, fruit, and gifts to take home.
items.meta: Wed · Fri · Sun · evenings · Mueang district

items.name: Evening Market at Lotus Tha Luang
items.blurb: An evening market in front of Lotus Tha Luang in town, handy if you're staying nearby. It has food and household goods at good prices, so you can graze before or after shopping inside the store on the same trip.

items.name: Je Khiad Market, Sak Lek Bus Terminal
items.blurb: A large Saturday market next to the Sak Lek bus terminal, very spacious with lots of food and packed crowds in the evening. A good alternative if you're out toward Sak Lek district or want a change from the in-town markets.
items.meta: Every Saturday · 3–8 pm · Sak Lek district

items.name: Bueng Si Fai at Night
items.blurb: A waterfront plaza at Bueng Si Fai where push-carts and food stalls set up in the evening. You can eat while catching the cool breeze off the water, with the giant Chalawan statue as a backdrop. It's better for chilling after dinner than for a serious meal, but it's a spot locals love to come stroll in the evening.
items.meta: Evening–night · Mueang district (near Bueng Si Fai)

blocks.title: Planning tip
blocks.html: Early in the week, the in-town markets are quieter on weekdays. If you stay over a Friday–Saturday you can hit both Bang Khi Nak Walking Street and Wang Krot Old Market on the same trip. From Wednesday to Sunday, Je Khiad Market at Sri Wanit in town is your reliable standby for an easy dinner.

Phichit's market food isn't flashy, but it's filling and friendly on the wallet. We've broken it down so you know what to look for when you arrive, from proper meals to snacks you carry and eat as you walk.

items.name: Rice-and-curry cart
items.blurb: The heart of a Phichit night market. The rice-and-curry stalls line up trays for you to pick what goes over your rice, from red curry and stir-fries to omelets and local dishes like the sour bamboo-shoot curry (kaeng nor som) that's a regional specialty. Two toppings over rice fills you up for under fifty.

items.name: Fried snacks — spring rolls, fried chicken, fried banana
items.blurb: Fried-snack stalls are a fixture of the night market: crispy spring rolls, fried chicken, fried sweet potato, fried banana, and fried taro, all hot out of the oil to carry and eat as you walk. Prices start at 20 THB a bag, making them the perfect companion to a market stroll.

items.name: Noodles & hand-pulled egg noodles
items.blurb: Plenty of markets have noodle and wonton carts with fresh-blanched noodles and homemade broth. Some vendors pull their own egg noodles, giving them a chewy, springy bite. A light meal before you graze on the rest.

items.name: Grilled skewers — pork, meatballs, Isan sausage
items.blurb: Grill stalls with charcoal braziers send out the smell from the entrance: grilled pork with sticky rice, grilled meatballs, and Isan sausage are popular snacks you'll find at nearly every market. Prices start around 10 THB a skewer.

items.name: Som tam & spicy salads
items.blurb: Papaya-salad stalls are another night-market staple: Thai-style som tam, fermented-fish som tam, and grilled pork neck pair with sticky rice and grilled chicken for a full meal. The flavors run bold the way people around here like them, but you can ask for less spice if you can't handle the heat.

blocks.html: What sets Phichit's markets apart from the rest is the old-fashioned local sweets you can still find around the old markets and walking streets. Many are regional treats the province is working to preserve, so if you spot them, give them a try — they get rarer by the year.

items: Khanom Khao Tu — an old-school sweet made from roasted rice mixed with sugar and coconut, fragrant, sweet, and soft. A celebrated Phichit local treat.
Khao Taen with young coconut — crispy fried sticky-rice crackers drizzled with sugar and topped with young coconut, crisp and sweet and easy to keep nibbling.
Fried lotus seeds — a regional snack made with lotus seeds from the province's lakes, fried crisp, fragrant, and rich.
Khanom Khao Pong / Khanom Khui Nu — hard-to-find old-fashioned sweets you can still come across at Wang Krot Old Market.
Tha Khoi pomelo — Phichit's famous fruit, firm-fleshed and sweet-tart, sold both fresh and processed into three-flavor dried pomelo to take home.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Some local sweets aren't sold at every market every day. Your best shot at finding the full range is Wang Krot Old Market and Bang Khi Nak Walking Street, while the general in-town markets lean more toward everyday eats and fried snacks. Don't expect to find every old-fashioned treat at a single market.

items.name: Three-flavor dried pomelo
items.blurb: Processed pomelo tossed with chili-salt and plum, tangy-sweet-salty and moreish. A lightweight gift you can pick up at souvenir shops and markets.

items.name: Phichit rice
items.blurb: Phichit is rice country, so milled rice and rice-based products make a gift you can carry home without weighing down your bag.

items.name: Bagged local sweets
items.blurb: Khao tu, khao taen, and fried lotus seeds — buy them bagged from the old market as a gift you won't find in Bangkok.

faq.q: Which days do Phichit's walking streets open?
faq.a: Bang Khi Nak Walking Street in Bang Mun Nak district opens every Saturday, 2–8 pm. In town, Je Khiad Market at Sri Wanit opens Wednesday to Sunday in the evening, and Wang Krot Old Market is busiest Friday–Saturday from midday into the afternoon. It's worth double-checking each market's page before you go, as days and hours can shift with the season.

faq.q: Where's the best night market to eat at in Phichit town?
faq.a: If you're staying in the city center, Je Khiad Market by the PTT station at Sri Wanit (Wed–Sun, 5–8 pm) is the most convenient, with a full spread of rice-and-curry, noodles, and fried snacks. On Saturdays you also have the evening market at Lotus Tha Luang and the Phichit Thani bus terminal market to choose from.

faq.q: What are the best eats at Phichit's markets?
faq.a: The staples are budget-friendly rice-and-curry over rice, fresh-fried snacks like spring rolls and fried banana, grilled pork and meatball skewers, and som tam. If you want to try regional dishes, look for the sour bamboo-shoot curry (kaeng nor som) and local sweets like khao tu, khao taen with young coconut, and fried lotus seeds.

faq.q: Is Wang Krot Old Market worth a visit?
faq.a: It's worth it if you like the atmosphere of an old riverside community and old-fashioned food. It's a district of wooden shophouses from the reign of King Rama V with plenty of hard-to-find local sweets gathered in one place. It's busiest Friday–Saturday from late morning into the afternoon, and many items sell out fast, so go before 3 pm.

faq.q: How much does a night of eating at Phichit's markets cost?
faq.a: You can eat comfortably on 100–150 THB per person. Rice-and-curry over rice runs about 35–55 THB, while fried snacks and grilled skewers start at 10–20 THB a piece. Add a little for sweets and a drink and you can graze all evening without straining your wallet.
